FINAL ENVIRONMENTAL STATEMENT ON THE PROPOSED ENDANGERED SPECIES CONSERVATION ACT OF 1973
I. DESCRIPTION OF THE PROPOSED ACTION
Under the proposed legislation the Endangered Species Conservation

Act of 1969 would be repealed, but the effect would be incremental to

present authority. This result would be known as the Endangered Species

Conservation Act of 1973. Following is a discussion of the changes in

present authority provided by the proposed Endangered Species Conservation

Act of 1973 as well as a review of present authority.
At the present time the term "endangered" as used in the Act is defined to mean those species and subspecies that are imminently threatened with extinction. Under the proposed legislation, endangered is considerably broadened to include not only those animals threatened with extinction but also any species or subspecies "likely within the foreseeable future to become threatened with extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range" (Appendix A). Such a change will enable the Secretary to take action to prevent the depletion of such species or subspecies to the point where they become endangered, as presently defined.
The term "significant portion" of its range is used in the definition of endangered to provide the Secretary with the authority to protect a population unique to some portion of the country without regard to its taxonomic status, or a population that is now endangered over a large portion of its range even if the population inhabiting that portion of the range is not recognized as a distinct subspecies from a more abundant population occurring elsewhere.
